mappings.note: Why corrosion is a problem -- the everyday consequences of metal oxidation, LO-2.
Names rust from its description. LO-2's corrosion clause; no reaction type is being classified, so not LO-1.
Rusting classified as corrosion (a slow oxidation) -- exactly what LO-2 names.
Both air and moisture needed for rusting -- the conditions for corrosion, LO-2.
Black coating on silver traced to H2S in air -- tarnishing, i.e. corrosion of a metal, LO-2.
Green coating on copper identified as its corrosion product, LO-2.
Groups silver tarnish and copper patina under corrosion -- LO-2's category.
Engineering consequence of corrosion -- the everyday-life clause of LO-2.
Economic loss from corrosion. Still LO-2's everyday effects of oxidation; no reaction is classified.
Why iron is painted or galvanised -- corrosion prevention, LO-2.
Names rancidity from the oxidation of fats and oils -- LO-2 verbatim.
Stale, foul-smelling chips diagnosed as rancidity, LO-2.
Cause of rancidity is oxidation by air -- LO-2's rancidity clause.
Method of preventing rancidity in packaged food, LO-2.
Nitrogen flushing to exclude oxygen and stop rancidity, LO-2.
Refrigeration slows the oxidation that causes rancidity -- LO-2, not an energy-change item.
Explains colour change and gas evolution as indicators that a reaction has occurred. This frame has no outcome for reaction indicators -- LO-1 is about naming reaction TYPES -- so competency level.
Reads a change of state and a temperature rise as indicators of reaction. Same frame gap as qid:700322; the warmth also falls in the energy-change gap.

Generic reaction-indicator recall. Mapped with the whole 705817-705856 indicator cluster to the competency, because no LO in this frame covers recognising that a reaction occurred as distinct from naming its type.
The term for the white insoluble solid from two solutions is 'precipitate'. Precipitation is the double-displacement clause of LO-1, so this one leaves the indicator cluster for a real outcome.
Which change is OBSERVED when magnesium burns. The construct is the observation, not the oxidation label, so the indicator competency rather than LO-1.
Souring of milk as a chemical change -- physical-versus-chemical judgement, no LO available.
Which observation is not by itself proof of a reaction -- indicator reliability, competency level.
The observation when dilute HCl meets zinc. Stays with the indicator cluster because the item asks what is SEEN, not what type of reaction it is.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic. Energy classification, which has no learning outcome in this frame.
Lime water turning milky. A gas-test observation; this frame has no outcome for identification tests, so competency level, consistent with qid:84850.
Candle burning involves both physical and chemical change -- the physical/chemical gap, competency level.
Which item is NOT one of the standard indications of a reaction -- indicator recall, competency level.
Recognising rusting by its reddish-brown coating is corrosion knowledge, so LO-2 rather than the generic indicator competency used for the rest of this cluster.
Which pair shows only a change of state -- distinguishing physical change, competency level.
Antacid bubbles as evidence of gas evolution. Indicator reasoning, no LO fits.
Defines a physical change as one forming no new substance. No LO in this frame covers physical versus chemical change.
What to conclude from a yellow solid appearing. The item is about drawing a conclusion from an observation, not naming the precipitation reaction, so the indicator competency.
Which observation shows chemical change when an iron nail sits in CuSO4. The displacement is only the setting; the question asks which observation is decisive.
A hot beaker on slaking lime shows the reaction is exothermic -- the energy-change gap, competency level.
Counts how many indications of chemical change are present. Purely indicator arithmetic, no LO.
Evaluates a claim that dissolving salt is a chemical change -- physical/chemical discrimination, competency level.
Which pair of observations most strongly suggests a chemical rather than physical change. Indicator reliability, no LO.
Which observation indicates chemical change when AgCl greys. The decomposition is the setting; the asked-for answer is the colour-change indicator.
Two cold test tubes mean both reactions are endothermic -- the energy-change gap.
Which everyday observation is caused by a chemical change -- physical/chemical discrimination, competency level.
Names the indicators present when a mixture bubbles and cools. Indicator identification, no LO.
The glow when iron and sulphur are heated as an indicator of reaction. Competency level with the rest of the cluster.
Which observation would cast doubt on a reaction having occurred -- indicator reliability, no LO.
Identifying CO2 by the lime water test. Gas identification tests have no outcome in this frame, so the competency.
Warmth alone with no other sign: evaluates a false negative. Indicator reasoning plus energy change, both outside this frame's LOs.
Burning magnesium versus rusting iron: the answer is that rusting is a SLOW oxidation, which is LO-2's corrosion content, so this item earns an outcome rather than the indicator competency.
One tube warms and one cools with the same mass of solid -- an energy-change inference, no LO available.
Evaporation versus burning, both leaving a residue. Physical/chemical discrimination, competency level.
A sealed flask showing no mass change is a direct demonstration of conservation of mass, so this leaves the indicator cluster for C 1.3-LO-2.
A lighter residue after gas escapes does NOT disprove conservation of mass -- LO-2's reasoning applied to an open system, not an indicator question.
Assertion-reason on whether a colour change always proves a reaction. Indicator reliability, competency level.

Best experimental design to separate physical from chemical change. Investigative design under the C 1.2 competency ('investigates the nature and properties of chemical substances'); C 8.1 is about building models, which is not what is asked.
The criticism is that heating copper carbonate is a DECOMPOSITION, not combustion. Naming the reaction type is LO-1, so this item leaves the indicator cluster.
When one observation is not enough to conclude a reaction occurred -- indicator reliability, competency level.
Warming as the only evidence in an acid-base mixing. Temperature indicator plus energy change, both outside this frame's LOs.
Two bubbling reactions distinguished by the lime water test. Gas identification, competency level, as with qid:705843.
Evaluates the claim that every reaction shows at least one of the five indications -- the limits of indicator evidence, competency level.
Reactants sit left of the arrow. Word-equation notation, so the C 1.3 competency; C 1.3-LO-1 is specifically about a BALANCED equation with physical states, neither of which a word equation carries.
How the arrow is read. Equation notation at word-equation level, so the competency.
Correct word equation for magnesium and oxygen -- constructing a word equation, competency level.
The plus sign separating reactants. Notation convention, C 1.3.
What a word equation does NOT show (formulae, quantities, states). A limitation of the notation, so the competency rather than C 1.3-LO-1.
Reads the products out of a given word equation -- interpreting the notation, C 1.3.
Which candidate is correctly written as a word equation. Notation correctness, competency level.
Constructing the rusting word equation (C 1.3) turns on knowing that BOTH oxygen and water are reactants, which is LO-2's corrosion condition, so both are cited.
Advantage of a word equation over prose -- the value of the representation, C 1.3.
Counts reactants in a given word equation. Reading the notation, competency level.
Which statement about word equations is true. Properties of the notation, C 1.3.
Picking the solid product of lead nitrate and potassium iodide needs the precipitation knowledge of LO-1 as well as reading the word equation (C 1.3).
What a word equation cannot be used to calculate. A limitation of the notation, so C 1.3 and not C 1.3-LO-2, which is about why balancing is required.
Meaning of the plus sign on the product side. Notation convention, C 1.3.
Correct word equation for sodium in water -- constructing the representation, competency level.
Which reactant is reduced in copper oxide plus hydrogen. Despite sitting in the word-equation set, the assessed skill is redox identification, which is LO-1.
Correct word equation for the thermal decomposition of limestone. The type is supplied in the stem, so only the equation is assessed: C 1.3, not LO-1.
Asks which word equation shows a metal displacing another metal -- explicit displacement classification (LO-1) read off a word equation (C 1.3).
What the word 'Heat' on the product side means. C 8.1-LO-1 names interpretation of the heat symbol specifically, which no other code does.
Identifying barium sulphate as the white insoluble product is the precipitation clause of LO-1; reading it out of the word equation is C 1.3.
Which sentence yields three reactants. Counting species while constructing a word equation, C 1.3.
Converting a sentence about slaking lime into a word equation and naming the product -- equation construction, C 1.3.
A word equation written back to front is wrong. Notation convention, competency level.
The KBr/BaI2 word equation is to be recognised as a double displacement -- LO-1 classification, with the word equation only supplying the data.
Which sentence gives a single product. The task is counting products while writing the equation, so C 1.3; the underlying combination reaction is not what is asked for.
Why chemists move from word to symbol equations. A comparison of representations, C 1.3.
Names the displaced element in Lead + Copper chloride. Displacement identification, LO-1.
Only the iron-displaces-copper direction is valid, because displacement runs one way down the reactivity series. LO-1's displacement clause.
Choosing between two proposed word equations requires knowing the actual products. The item is about what a written equation must be grounded in, so C 1.3.
Two reactants, two products and no free element rules out displacement. Reaction-type discrimination, LO-1.
A word equation can be right yet useless for yield because it carries no formulae or amounts. A limitation of the representation, so C 1.3.
Whether heat written on the left always means endothermic -- interpreting the heat notation, which C 8.1-LO-1 names.
The risk in converting 'AgCl turns grey in sunlight' is writing sunlight as a reactant instead of a condition. That is a word-equation construction error, C 1.3.
Why two correct accounts can list different numbers of reactants -- equation construction judgement, C 1.3.
One reactant giving three products points to decomposition. The item asks for the reaction TYPE, so LO-1 rather than the notation competency.
Criticising 'Acid + Base -> Salt + Water' as too generic to be a real word equation -- a critique of the representation, C 1.3.
What to do when a product cannot be named while writing a word equation -- equation construction practice, C 1.3.
A word equation stays valid unbalanced because it carries no quantities. Cited at C 1.3 and not C 1.3-LO-2: the point is what word equations omit, not why symbol equations must be balanced.
What the photosynthesis word equation hides (conditions, amounts). A limitation of the representation, C 1.3.
